title: “No Singing in the Navy” runs through April 19th at Playwrights Horiz...
transcript: it's kind of like if SpongeBob Squarepants critiqued military propaganda and wartime patriotism through the lens of Golden Age musicals the silliest show in New York right now is this small scale musical comedy which kind of borrows the basic premise of the musical On The Town: three sailors on leave in the big city for just one day or as they frequently put it in the show “24 Hours until we die” it features talking crabs Looney Tunes antics and of course, a lot of singing against the titular command of their grumpy naval captain this particular brand of absurdity which, like I said, felt almost in the vein of something like SpongeBob where it's very cartoonish but with a weird edge to it it's very much my sense of humor I found myself laughing giddily through most of the show but as much as the show is quite silly it also seems to question what silliness itself even is. there's like a darker philosophical underbelly here not just because the characters are facing their own death but through sometimes jarring interludes of reflection on their sense of self what does it mean to be a conscious human with agency and not just a silly sailor in a musical? and it's in this question that the writer, Milo Cramer, folds in this examination of musical theatre as an art form not quite in the intuitive way that you would expect; rather than just satirizing the way early musicals like On the Town might have been complicit in the military propaganda machine Cramer sort of leap-frogs that straightforward angle and instead uses these philosophical tangents to question the two faces of musical theatre throughout history sometimes highlighting a character's humanity and sometimes flattening it into a cheap archetype. which in turn can prompt us to question whether mainstream musical theatre today is really challenging this systems in place or reinforcing them. that's what I got from it anyway but the commentary is admittedly more opaque than you might expect. on a story level it veers into these vignette-like subplots that don't offer a clear sense of direction or purpose even within the framework of absurdist comedy so I'd be lying if I said I didn't feel kind of bemused at certain points throughout but even in those moments I was pretty captivated by the intersection of these strange fever dreams in conversation with irresistibly delightful comedy so if you want a more straightforward parody of classic musicals I would probably wait for Schmigadoon but if you're up for something a little stranger I would recommend this one but I should add the disclaimer that I have like five or six other friends who have seen this and none of them liked it as much as I did and I get it I really do but I don't know I dug it
